about: Roughness: how two simultaneous partials beat against each other as heard, by their frequencies. Read by the spectral harmonic system's roughness (public/shared/harmonic-systems/spectral.js) and the harmony's spectral consonance (public/shared/estimation/spectral-consonance.js), each weighting a pair of partials by their amplitudes as it chooses. A measure of sensory roughness, not of musical quality.

dissonance-curve.unit: b1, b2: per unit of s times hertz; dStar: the curve's peak, in units of s times hertz; s1: per hertz; s2: hertz
dissonance-curve.where: the dissonance curve d(x) = exp(-b1 s x) - exp(-b2 s x), s = dStar / (s1 f + s2), for two partials x hertz apart above the lower at f hertz, as harmonic-systems/spectral.js had its parameters from the paper (the full text not saved: research/SOURCES_TO_FETCH.md); spectral-consonance.js had s1 and s2 rounded (0.021, 19)
dissonance-curve.conditions: fitted to Plomp and Levelt's (1965) judgements of the consonance of two simultaneous pure tones, by their frequency difference, at several mean frequencies
dissonance-curve.note: the roughness of two pure tones: none in unison, rising to its most at about a quarter of a critical band apart and falling away past it, the band widening with frequency. Summed over the partials of two complex tones it is Sethares's extension to timbres, and over instruments' spectra ours
